reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight of the paper lies in applying Bayesian Structural Time Series (BSTS) to decompose betting market probabilities into two components: a latent random walk trend (signal) and Gaussian noise (noise). The signal component τ² captures persistent drift due to informed trading, while the noise component σ² reflects short-term fluctuations. In GSI, this translates to modeling voter intent through market prices, where τ²/σ² quantifies the reliability of implied probabilities. For GSE, the same framework models NFL line movements, treating each game’s odds as a time series subject to similar signal-noise dynamics. The local-level BSTS model assumes that the underlying trend μ_t evolves randomly over time, which aligns with how game states evolve unpredictably. Forecasting proceeds by projecting μ_t forward using past observations, producing predictive intervals that reflect uncertainty. This approach enables both systems to respond dynamically to new information, such as polling shifts or injury reports, while maintaining statistical rigor through Bayesian updating. However, the method suffers from potential adversarial manipulation—such as large whale bets—which can distort the signal. To address this, an extension incorporating jump detection is proposed, allowing for robust identification of true steam versus artificial inflation.
